captions.speaker: Maya

captions.text: The blog itself is a little mystery. The archive shows exactly one post.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: But distance does something stranger, too—it enlarges the ordinary. That's where we're headed next.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: It takes every ordinary thing you left behind and makes it radiant.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: And what he's longing for isn't grand at all. It's voices. Songs. Faces.

captions.text: He pictures himself on a little island in the boundless ocean, surrounded by travelers gambling over champagne on a Sunday.

captions.speaker: Maya

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: He is also harsh about foreign faces and tongues in ways that are very much of his era. That's his period-bound lens, not ours.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: But that impulse — cataloguing exactly what you miss — it doesn't go away. A blogger named Emily does the same thing in 2012, from Kenya.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: She's on a site called One Trailing Spouse, and she writes this list of five things she misses about the U.S. after five months abroad.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: And the list is so specific it's almost funny.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: How specific are we talking?

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Purple corduroy pants. Her muffin tin. Netflix.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: The muffin tin is the one that gets me.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: And driving — just the freedom to get in a car by herself after dark. She's candid that this is a privileged perspective, she says so.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: But missing the feeling of casual safety? That's real no matter how you frame it.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: A commenter named Marina chimes in from England and says she hasn't worn completely dry clothes in nearly two years. She misses the sun. And avocados.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Honestly? Avocados can do that.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: Then there's Kathleen, on a WordPress blog called My 8×10 Life. She grew up in the rural Midwest, moved reluctantly to Brooklyn.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: And she writes about driving back through those Midwestern landscapes and feeling like she could finally stretch and breathe again — after months of swallowing the grit of New York.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: But she says something that really gets me. She talks about the details of home growing fuzzy, and it bothers her.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Like the feelings of belonging are still sharp, but the specifics — they're slipping away.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: But, I don’t think I’ll ever allow myself to like it, and will never love it no matter how well I adapt to the urban life. I guess it makes me feel disloyal to my roots.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Disloyal. That word. Homesickness isn't just missing a place — it becomes a kind of moral obligation to keep missing it.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: We found another exile — a memoir fragment from the Internet Archive's OCR pipeline. Someone marking a thirty-seventh birthday in May 1919, living in seclusion on an island.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: The narrator doesn't fully identify themselves in this fragment, but letters and flowers arrive from Germany — so many the small rooms of a parsonage can't hold them all.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: What struck me is how the narrator measures belonging — not by being present, but by being remembered.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: Those letters prove people still feel connected across distance and, as the writer puts it, across a wildly raging campaign of slander.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: And we should be honest — we don't know from this fragment alone who the narrator is or what the slander was about. The text starts mid-sentence.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: That's the nature of digitized scraps.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: A gap is not permission to invent.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: Which brings us to a passage that kind of names the whole feeling we've been circling.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: From what appears to be volume twenty-one of the collected works of someone abbreviated 'Stev' in the filename — an essay about roads.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: And the writer introduces this German word: Sehnsucht.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: The passion for what is ever beyond. That ache for the horizon.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: And the essay quotes Goethe's Werther to make a devastating point.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: When you finally reach the distance you wanted—when 'there' becomes 'here'—everything is afterwards as it was before.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: So arrival can make the dream smaller?

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Exactly. You arrive, and the magic collapses.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: Wheeler sighing for home voices. Kathleen gripping the steering wheel through flat fields.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: Emily dreaming of purple pants. The unnamed exile counting birthday flowers.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: They're all living inside that word: Sehnsucht.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: But Sehnsucht changes when the distant place becomes a destination. What happens when you actually go back?

captions.speaker: Maya

captions.speaker: Lina

captions.text: And that's what shaped how she saw home. She writes that she'd grown to hate the mountains—the whole town.

captions.text: Homecoming as time travel.

captions.text: So we've talked about leaving and coming back. But here's what nobody warns you about.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: And that raises a real question—who gets to define a place's identity? The person who left, or the people who live there now?

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: The person who stayed might answer very differently.

captions.text: That's the tension. The Iowa and Texas writers grieve what's gone but hold it lightly—they know the loss is partly theirs, inside them.

captions.speaker: Maya

captions.text: What strikes me across all of these is that no one finds what they went back for.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: So what do you do with the love that has nowhere to land?

captions.text: Sometimes the place can't hold the love, so a smell, a logo, or an old object does. That's where these stories take us next.

captions.text: And his schoolhouse — a log hut with windows made by cutting out a log and pasting oiled paper over the hole.

captions.text: That's the landscape these people are building memory from.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: Which brings us to someone who grew up in a landscape most people wouldn't think to feel nostalgic about at all.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: A professor named Michael Rustad, writing about the Red River Valley in northwestern Minnesota — flat black-loam prairie, endless horizon.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: I grew up longing to leave the flat land.

captions.text: And what changed him was a sixth-grade teacher — Dale Finney Miller — who taught Scandinavian mythology and local history, the Alexandria runestone, stories about the land under his feet.

captions.text: This essay was written in 2001, posted on a RootsWeb genealogy page — hand-coded HTML, no content-management system — and crawled twelve years later in December 2013.

captions.text: The extraction cuts off mid-sentence too. He was about to say something about learning from his teachers, and then — nothing. The crawler just stopped.

captions.text: Again?

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Every one of these people — the blogger, the minister, Nichols, Rustad — the archive caught them.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: But it can't give us back the alligator logo, or the minister's full name, or the end of Rustad's sentence.

captions.text: So we've been sitting with all these places people leave behind, and the things they build to hold onto them.

captions.text: I want to end with a guy who did something I find kind of beautiful. He named his whole company after a park.

captions.text: And his about-us page—crawled December 2013—has this origin story: when he was a kid in Connecticut, there was a park called PineRock Park. Baseball, live music, giant swings.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: He named the future after the feeling.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: I didn't know what I wanted to be when I grew up, but I did know that I wanted to create something that moved me in that same way. And I decided that when I did, I would call it PineRock.

captions.text: Okay, yes, it's a corporate page—it's branding. But the impulse underneath it is real.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: You take a childhood feeling and pour it into a name so it outlives the place itself.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: He calls himself an amateur semiotician.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: On a blog about Smurfs.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: Which is a wonderful sentence.

captions.speaker: Maya
captions.text: But then he says his year has been rough. And Halloween is the one season where he can let go and just feel something good.

captions.text: He ends up at a Yankee Candle browsing the Boney Bunch collection with his spouse, and the blog entry literally cuts off mid-sentence during that visit.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: And there goes the sentence again.

captions.text: Fragments keep being the theme. There's a poem on PoetrySoup by Andrew Nashat called "Do you remember."

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: We only have a name on a community poetry site; we don't know more about the writer.

captions.speaker: Theo
captions.text: The whole poem is built on that phrase, repeated like a heartbeat.

captions.speaker: Lina
captions.text: I remember the days when all we wanted to do was be together, I remember the days when all we wanted to do was be there for each other, I remember the days when all we did was reminisce our childhood memories, I remember those days my dear.

captions.text: since I left my fatherland, you are one of those to whom my heart specially clings.

captions.text: Then he says he has to withdraw from everyone because of his hearing loss.

captions.text: The people he most wants to reach are the very people he is being pulled away from.

captions.text: It can't give back the thing that was reached for.

captions.speaker: Theo

captions.text: And they wanted something badly enough to write it down.
